title: Nonlinear dynamics of random neural networks with second-order synaptic motifs
abstract: Classical theories of random neural networks typically assume independent connectivity, overlooking the local motif structures prevalent in biological circuits. Here, we investigate how four second-order synaptic motifs (chain, reciprocal, convergent, and divergent) shape the dynamics of nonlinear firing-rate networks. While previous studies have established that chain correlations generate outlier eigenvalues, we demonstrate that these motifs also jointly reshape the Jacobian eigenvalue bulk. Using the path-integral formalism, we derive a dynamic mean-field theory which reveals that the chain motif acts as a retarded feedback of the ensemble-mean activity through the response kernel, producing a rich repertoire of dynamical regimes, including ferromagnetic states and limit cycles. At sufficiently large magnitude, negative chain correlations produce a glassy, multistable regime that was previously mainly associated with partially symmetric networks. Our theory also distinguishes convergent from divergent motifs: divergent correlations primarily rescale temporal noise, while convergent correlations suppress temporal chaos by converting nonzero mean activity into quenched heterogeneity. Finally, analyses of the Lyapunov spectrum and participation-ratio dimension show that motif structure changes the geometry of chaotic activity, reducing entropy production and attractor dimensionality even when the effective spectral edge is held fixed. Together, these findings establish second-order motifs as a fundamental structural mechanism governing the dynamical regimes of local cortical circuits.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes how specific local synaptic motifs in neural networks modify their collective dynamics using Dynamic Mean-Field Theory. The study shows that these motifs are not merely minor perturbations but fundamental structural elements that dictate the network's dynamical regimes, ranging from stable oscillations to glassy states. This establishes motif structure as a key determinant of cortical circuit function.
main_problem: The paper investigates how specific local synaptic motif structures (chain, reciprocal, convergent, divergent) influence the nonlinear dynamics of random neural networks, moving beyond models assuming independent connectivity.
main_result: These second-order motifs fundamentally reshape the network's Jacobian eigenvalue bulk and dictate rich dynamical regimes, such as ferromagnetic states, limit cycles, and glassy dynamics, by acting as structural constraints on activity.
method: The authors employ Dynamic Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) and the path-integral formalism to derive theoretical predictions about the network's spectral properties and long-time dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is a nonlinear firing-rate network modeled by the Sompolinsky–Crisanti–Sommers (SCS) equation. Connectivity is generalized Gaussian, incorporating correlations defined by four second-order synaptic motifs.
key_observables: Jacobian eigenvalue bulk and outliers, effective gain ($g_{	ext{eff}}$), Lyapunov spectrum, participation-ratio dimension, and dynamical regimes (e.g., ferromagnetic states, limit cycles).
important_parameters: The Pearson correlation coefficients ($	au$) characterizing the four motifs ($	au_{	ext{chn}}, 	au_{	ext{rec}}, 	au_{	ext{con}}, 	au_{	ext{div}}$) are the key structural parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the connectivity entries are jointly Gaussian, and the theory extends the DMFT framework to incorporate these motif correlations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the four motifs and shows how motif correlations affect the eigenvalue bulk and outliers of the Jacobian.
paper_structure: The paper develops a dynamic mean-field theory by incorporating motif correlations into the network dynamics. It analyzes the resulting spectral changes, detailing how positive and negative chain correlations lead to distinct dynamical instabilities, and separately analyzes the roles of convergent and divergent motifs on chaos and noise.
why_interesting: The detailed mathematical framework connecting local structural motifs to global dynamical stability (eigenvalues, chaos) provides a powerful, structured analogy to how local interactions govern emergent behavior in complex quantum many-body systems or disordered quantum materials.
